title: What the Internet Is
summary: How your message reaches a server across the world in an instant.

pages.title: A network of networks
pages.body:
The internet is a giant network connecting millions of smaller networks: home Wi-Fi, office networks, mobile carriers, and data centers.

Devices on the internet usually act as:
- Client: the one asking (your phone opening an app)
- Server: the one answering (the computer holding the app's data)

Every time you open a site, your phone (the client) sends a request and the server sends a response.
pages.tip: The client is a shopper, the server is the shopkeeper. The shopper asks; the shopkeeper prepares and hands over the order.

pages.title: Data is split into packets
pages.body:
Data isn't sent in one piece. A 2 MB photo is cut into thousands of small packets, each with a sender and destination address.

Those packets:
- Can take different routes
- Can arrive out of order and get reassembled at the destination
- Get resent if any go missing

Routers along the way decide where to forward each packet.
pages.tip: Like shipping a wardrobe: it's taken apart into numbered boards, sent separately, then reassembled at the destination.

pages.title: Who's along the route
pages.body:
One request's journey from your phone:
- Phone → home Wi-Fi router or cell tower
- → ISP (your internet provider, e.g. a mobile carrier)
- → several routers between networks
- → the destination server

That means many parties sit along the way. That's why encryption (HTTPS) matters: those in the middle only see the envelope, not its contents.
pages.tip: Your packet is like a letter passed through many post offices. That's why its contents must be sealed.

quiz.prompt: When you open a news app, your phone acts as the...
quiz.explanation: The device requesting data is the client; the one providing it is the server.

quiz.prompt: Why is data sent as small packets?
options: So they can take different routes and be resent if lost
Because phones can't handle big files
quiz.explanation: Small packets are more flexible and resilient than one big transfer.

quiz.prompt: A router's job is to...
quiz.explanation: A router reads a packet's destination and chooses the next hop.

quiz.prompt: An ISP is...
quiz.explanation: An ISP is the company that connects you to the internet.

quiz.prompt: Why does HTTPS matter when data passes through many parties?
options: Parties in the middle can't read the contents
quiz.explanation: Encryption keeps contents secret even across many routers and networks.

title: IP Addresses
summary: Every device's home address on a network: public, private, IPv4, and IPv6.

pages.title: IPv4 and IPv6
pages.body:
An IP address is a number that identifies a device on a network.

- IPv4: four numbers from 0–255 separated by dots, e.g. 192.168.1.10. About 4.3 billion addresses in total, which ran short long ago
- IPv6: longer, using hexadecimal and colons, e.g. 2001:db8::1. Practically unlimited

Modern phones usually have both at once.
pages.tip: IPv4 is house numbers in a small, full neighborhood. IPv6 is a giant new neighborhood with room for everyone.

pages.title: Private vs public IP
pages.body:
Not every address is visible from the internet.

- Private IP: only valid on a local network. The ranges are 10.x.x.x, 172.16–31.x.x, and 192.168.x.x
- Public IP: the address seen on the internet, usually belonging to your home router or carrier

Routers use NAT to translate many private IPs into one public IP. That's why the phone, laptop, and TV at home reach the internet with the same public IP.
pages.tip: A private IP is a hotel room number. The public IP is the hotel's address. Couriers only know the hotel; the receptionist (NAT) delivers to the room.

pages.title: What an IP reveals
pages.body:
A public IP can give a rough picture:
- City or region (often inaccurate)
- The internet provider you use

But an IP doesn't show your exact home address. Only the ISP can match an IP to a customer, usually only through legal process.

See your phone's own private IP in Toolbox → Network Info.
pages.tip: An IP is like a postal code. People can guess your area, but not which house is yours.

quiz.prompt: Which is a valid IPv4 address?
quiz.explanation: Each IPv4 part is 0–255. 300 is too big, and 2001:db8::1 is IPv6.

quiz.prompt: The address 192.168.0.5 is a...
quiz.explanation: The 192.168.x.x range is reserved for local networks.

quiz.prompt: NAT on a router is used to...
options: Translate many private IPs into one public IP
quiz.explanation: NAT lets many devices share a single public IP.

quiz.prompt: Why was IPv6 created?
quiz.explanation: IPv4 has only about 4.3 billion addresses, not enough for every device in the world.

quiz.prompt: From someone's public IP, others can usually learn...
options: A rough region and the ISP name
quiz.explanation: An IP gives only a rough picture. Customer data stays with the ISP.

title: Subnets Without Headaches
summary: Read /24 and /16, and tell the network part from the device part.

pages.title: Two parts in one IP
pages.body:
An IP address has two parts:
- Network part: identifies the "neighborhood"
- Host part: identifies the "house" or device inside it

A subnet mask or CIDR notation (/number) tells how many leading bits belong to the network. IPv4 has 32 bits in total.

Example 192.168.1.10/24: the first 24 bits (192.168.1) are the network, the remaining 8 bits (.10) are the device.
pages.tip: Like the address "Jasmine St, Block C, No. 10": "Block C" is the network, "No. 10" is the house.

pages.title: Counting addresses
pages.body:
The formula: number of addresses = 2 to the power of (32 minus the CIDR number).

- /24 → 2^8 = 256 addresses
- /16 → 2^16 = 65,536 addresses
- /30 → 2^2 = 4 addresses

In each subnet, 2 addresses are special:
- The first = the network address (e.g. 192.168.1.0)
- The last = broadcast (e.g. 192.168.1.255)

So a /24 has 254 addresses usable by devices.
pages.tip: A housing block has 256 plots, but the first is for the gate and the last for the guard post. That leaves 254 for houses.

pages.title: Why subnets matter for security
pages.body:
Subnets aren't just about counting. In security, they're used to separate networks:
- Guest Wi-Fi is kept apart from the office network
- CCTV cameras and smart devices are separated from work laptops
- Critical servers sit in their own subnet with strict firewall rules

If one device gets malware, spreading is harder because it's not in the same "neighborhood" as the others. This is called segmentation.
pages.tip: Like a ship with watertight compartments. One room floods, but the ship doesn't sink right away.

quiz.prompt: How many total addresses are in a /24 subnet?
How many addresses are usable by devices in a /24?
quiz.explanation: 256 minus the network and broadcast addresses = 254.

quiz.prompt: In 10.0.5.20/16, the network part is...
quiz.explanation: /16 means the first 16 bits, which is the first two numbers: 10.0.

quiz.prompt: How many total addresses does a /30 subnet have?
quiz.explanation: 2^(32-30) = 2^2 = 4 addresses (2 usable).

quiz.prompt: Separating guest Wi-Fi from the office network is called...
quiz.explanation: Segmentation limits how attacks spread between parts of a network.

title: DNS: The Internet's Phone Book
summary: From domain name to IP address, and how DNS can be abused.

pages.title: Easy names, hard numbers
pages.body:
Humans remember wikipedia.org easily, but computers need an IP address. DNS (Domain Name System) translates domain names into IPs.

The short version:
- Your phone asks a DNS resolver (usually your ISP's or a service like 1.1.1.1)
- The resolver asks a chain of servers up to the authoritative one
- The answer (an IP) comes back and is cached for a while

Try it yourself in Toolbox → Network Info → Try DNS.
pages.tip: DNS is your contact list. You look up "Mom"; the phone knows the number.

pages.title: Types of DNS records
pages.body:
A domain can have several record types:
- A: name → IPv4 address
- AAAA: name → IPv6 address
- CNAME: an alias pointing to another name
- MX: the mail server for that domain
- TXT: text notes, often used for verification and email anti-spam (SPF, DMARC)

Pentesters and analysts often check these records to map an organization's services.
pages.tip: DNS records are like a building directory: which floor an office is on, where the mailbox is, what else the building is called.

pages.title: When DNS is abused
pages.body:
Since almost every connection starts with DNS, attackers like to target it:
- DNS spoofing: a fake answer that sends you to a look-alike site
- A hacked home router whose DNS settings are changed
- Look-alike domains (typosquatting) registered on purpose by scammers

Defenses: change your router's admin password, use a trusted DNS resolver, check HTTPS and the site address, and turn on Private DNS on Android if needed.
pages.tip: If a prankster swapped your contact list, you'd call "Mom" and reach a scammer instead.

quiz.prompt: DNS's main job is to...
options: Translate domain names into IP addresses
quiz.explanation: DNS answers the question "what's the IP for this name?".

quiz.prompt: The DNS record pointing to a domain's mail server is...
quiz.explanation: MX (Mail Exchange) points to the mail server.

quiz.prompt: An AAAA record contains...
quiz.explanation: A is for IPv4, AAAA is for IPv6.

quiz.prompt: An attacker changes your home router's DNS settings. The effect?
options: You can be redirected to fake sites
quiz.explanation: A rogue DNS can point real site names to a scammer's server.

quiz.prompt: A simple step to protect your router from DNS hijacking?
quiz.explanation: Many routers are hacked because the default admin password was never changed.

title: Ports & Protocols
summary: One IP, many doors: ports, TCP vs UDP, and common services.

pages.title: Ports: doors on one address
pages.body:
One server can run many services at once: web, email, remote login. To keep them apart, each service "listens" on a different port number (0–65535).

A full destination = IP + port, e.g. 93.184.216.34:443.

On your phone's side, the system also picks a temporary random port for each outgoing connection.
pages.tip: The IP is the building's address; the port is the counter number. Counter 443 handles secure web, counter 25 handles mail.

pages.title: Ports worth knowing
pages.body:
Memorize a few that show up most:
- 22: SSH, encrypted remote login
- 53: DNS
- 80: HTTP (unencrypted web)
- 443: HTTPS (encrypted web)
- 25 / 587: sending email (SMTP)
- 3389: Windows Remote Desktop

A port open to the internet without need is a weakness. Attackers constantly hunt for servers with port 22 or 3389 using weak passwords.
pages.tip: Every open door is a chance for a thief to try. Doors you don't use, lock them.

pages.title: TCP vs UDP
pages.body:
The two main ways to send data:
- TCP: does a "handshake" first, checks every packet arrives, and resends missing ones. Used for web, email, chat
- UDP: sends right away without checking. Faster, but some may be lost. Used for DNS, video calls, online games

The choice depends on the need: accuracy (TCP) or speed (UDP).
pages.tip: TCP is shipping with a courier who needs a signature. UDP is tossing flyers: fast, but nobody checks they arrived.

quiz.prompt: Port 443 is usually used for...
quiz.explanation: 443 is the standard port for encrypted web (HTTPS).

quiz.prompt: Which service usually runs on port 22?
quiz.explanation: Port 22 is used by SSH for encrypted remote login.

quiz.prompt: Why should unused ports be closed?
options: To reduce weaknesses attackers can target
quiz.explanation: Every exposed service is one more door for attackers.

quiz.prompt: The protocol that checks every packet arrives and resends missing ones is...
quiz.explanation: TCP guarantees data arrives complete and in order.

quiz.prompt: Video calls suit UDP because...
options: It's faster; losing a little data is fine
quiz.explanation: For live calls, delay is more annoying than losing a frame or two.

title: Linux & Terminal Basics
summary: Meet the terminal: folders, files, permissions, and root.

pages.title: Why Linux matters in cyber security
pages.body:
Most servers on the internet run Linux, Android is built on the Linux kernel, and nearly every security tool is designed for Linux.

On Linux, the most efficient way to work is the terminal: you type a command, the system runs it. It sounds old-school, but it's exactly what lets admins and security analysts work fast and precisely.
pages.tip: A GUI is driving an automatic; the terminal is a manual. Tricky at first, but you get full control.

pages.title: Basic commands
pages.body:
The ones you'll use most:
- pwd: which folder you're in
- ls: list a folder (ls -a for hidden files)
- cd name: change folder (cd .. to go up one level)
- cat file: read a file
- grep word file: find lines containing a word

Files or folders whose names start with a dot (.) are hidden. They're often settings files, and sometimes used to stash things that "shouldn't be seen".
pages.tip: pwd checks the "You are here" sign, ls looks inside the cupboard, cd moves rooms, cat opens and reads a letter.

pages.title: Permissions & root
pages.body:
Every file has permissions for three groups: owner, group, and others. Each can have:
- r (read)
- w (write)
- x (execute)

For example, -rw-r--r-- means the owner can read and write, everyone else can only read.

Root is the super account that can do anything. That's why daily work uses a normal account, and sudo only when truly needed. This principle is called least privilege.

Practice: open Toolbox → Terminal Simulator and find the hidden flag.
pages.tip: Root is the building's master key. Guards don't carry it every day, only in emergencies.

quiz.prompt: The command to show hidden files is...
quiz.explanation: The -a (all) option also shows files starting with a dot.

quiz.prompt: The pwd command shows...
quiz.explanation: pwd = print working directory.

quiz.prompt: The permission -rw-r--r-- means...
options: The owner can read and write, others can only read
quiz.explanation: The first three letters are the owner's (rw-), then group (r--), then others (r--).

quiz.prompt: The least privilege principle means...
options: Grant only the access that's needed
quiz.explanation: Minimal access limits the damage if an account is misused.

quiz.prompt: The command to find lines containing "error" in log.txt?
quiz.explanation: grep searches for a text pattern inside a file.
